title: ARM64
summary: ARM64 (AArch64) is a 64-bit extension of the ARM architecture introduced in 2011 with ARMv8-A. It adds a 64-bit execution state and the A64 instruction set alongside the existing 32-bit AArch32 state, enabling greater memory capacity and performance. The architecture maintains backward compatibility by supporting both 32-bit and 64-bit execution, allowing 32-bit applications to run on 64-bit operating systems. ARM64 includes enhanced SIMD (Neon) with 32 registers, dedicated cryptography instructions, and a new exception system. It is implemented in application processors like Cortex-A series and is mandatory in ARMv9-A. The 64-bit state uses 31 general-purpose registers and 32 128-bit SIMD registers, with addresses assumed 64-bit.

mechanisms.title: 64-bit Execution State and A64 Instruction Set
mechanisms.explanation: ARM64 introduces a distinct 64-bit execution state (AArch64) with the new A64 instruction set. This state provides 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers and 32 × 128-bit SIMD registers, replacing the 32-bit AArch32 state. It supports 64-bit addresses and instructions that can operate on 32-bit or 64-bit arguments, enabling larger memory spaces and faster calculations compared to 32-bit versions.

mechanisms.title: Backward Compatibility via AArch32 Coexistence
mechanisms.explanation: ARM64 is designed to work alongside the older 32-bit mode (AArch32), supporting both execution states within the same architecture. This allows 32-bit user-space applications to run on 64-bit operating systems and permits a 32-bit OS to operate under a 64-bit hypervisor. Processors may support one or both states at different exception levels, maintaining compatibility with existing 32-bit ARMv7-A software.
